title: Copy-as-Decode: Grammar-Constrained Parallel Prefill for LLM Editing

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Copy-as-Decode: Grammar-Constrained Parallel
Prefill for LLM Editing


Ziyang Liu
Independent Researcher
ziyang.liu.r@outlook.com

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Large language models edit text and code by autoregressively regenerating the
full output, even when most tokens appear verbatim in the input. We study a
decoding-layer mechanism, Copy-as-Decode, that recasts edit generation as structured decoding over a two-primitive grammar—<copy lines="i-j"/> references
an input line range, <gen> ... </gen> emits new content. A token-level FSM
guarantees syntactic validity, and a serving-layer primitive updates the KV cache
for each copy span via a single parallel-prefill forward rather than N autoregressive
steps, sharing the parallel-forward kernel of speculative decoding but with input
tokens as the draft and program-enforced acceptance in place of probabilistic verification. The contribution is the mechanism together with an upper-bound analysis
of its payoff that requires no end-to-end model training.
We report two quantitative bounds and one correctness property. (i) Kernel
speedup: on Qwen2.5-{1.5B, 7B}, copying N tokens via parallel prefill is 6.8×–
303× faster than emitting them autoregressively (N ∈ [8, 512], A100 80GB bf16).
(ii) Copy ceiling: on ProbeEdit and HumanEvalPack-Fix (Py/JS), 74–98% of gold
tokens are reachable under the line-level primitive; composed with the empirical
kernel s(N ) over each corpus’s exact span histogram this yields the closed-form
wall-clock bound bndexact = 29.0 × /3.4 × /4.2× (ProbeEdit / Py / JS; 13.0×
pooled). A token-level extension reaches 91–99% coverage with conservative
floors of 4.5–6.5×. (iii) Pipeline losslessness: oracle programs round-trip through
the deterministic resolver on all 482 cases, an identifiability precondition that
localizes any downstream failure to span selection rather than the mechanism.
A perturbation study shows pooled EM drops from 100% to 15.48% under offby-one noise, quantifying the span-selection precision required. A supervised
fine-tuning pilot on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (131–385 oracle programs, 3 seeds, 99
held-out attempts per configuration) lifts HEvalFix-Py EM from 0/33 (untrained,
any strategy) to 12–17% (Wilson 95% CI [7.0, 26.0]), a learnability signal, not a
production-accuracy span selector. We do not claim batched-serving integration or
agentic multi-file coverage; these are scoped as direct follow-up.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
LLM-based editing of text and code is pervasive—code-assistant apply loops, notebook rewrites,
collaborative document revision—yet the dominant serving strategy is wasteful. Given an input
document D and an instruction, the model emits the edited output D′ autoregressively, one token
at a time, from scratch. Because typical edits preserve most of D verbatim (e.g. 74–98% of gold
tokens reproducible from D under our line-level copy primitive, §4.2), most of those forward passes
regenerate content the model has already attended to in its prompt. This has two compounding costs:
wall-clock latency scales with output length, not with edit size, and the model is free to drift on tokens
that should have been fixed by the edit contract.
Preprint. Under review.

Figure 1: Mechanism comparison. (a) Standard autoregressive decoding spends one forward pass
per output token. (b) Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose k tokens that the target
model verifies in one parallel forward; tokens are accepted probabilistically. (c) Copy-as-Decode
degenerates the draft to the input document: a grammar-constrained decoder commits to a specific
<copy lines="i-j"/> span, and one parallel-prefill forward splices the corresponding N input
tokens into the KV cache with acceptance = 1 by construction. The kernel operation in (c) is the same
parallel forward used in (b)’s verifier, but with zero rejection risk inside a copy op. Full mechanism
in §2.

Scope of this paper. We study a decoding-layer mechanism, not a production editing system.
We (a) formulate the mechanism, (b) establish two quantitative upper bounds and one correctness
property—composed into a single span-distribution-aware exact bound bndexact (Table 2) that
holds independently of base-model quality, (c) characterize, via a controlled perturbation study,
the span-selection precision a downstream trained system would need to realize those bounds, and
(d) run a small-scale SFT pilot (§5) that reaches 12–17% mean-over-3-seeds held-out EM (95%
CI [7.0, 20.1] and [11.0, 26.0] respectively) at 1.5B on 131–385 examples—clearing the untrained
0% baseline decisively but below deployment. We do not integrate the splice with batched-serving
stacks (vLLM/SGLang) or evaluate on agentic multi-file workloads (SWE-bench-style); our endto-end spot-check on a 7B untrained base (Appendix P) places the current model relative to the
oracle ceiling but is not itself the efficiency claim. Prior work addresses edit serving only partly.
Search-and-replace formats [6] and unified diffs reduce output tokens but still re-emit structural
context through autoregressive decoding, and suffer anchor-ambiguity failures we quantify in §4.4
(search/replace round-trip-EM drops to 0.81–0.94 on our corpora where C OPY- AS -D ECODE remains
at 1.00). Speculative decoding [1, 13, 14, 28] accelerates free-form generation with probabilistic
acceptance but offers no token-identity guarantees on copy-heavy regions; production apply tools [4]
are trained on proprietary data and not directly reproducible. We take a simpler view: if 90%+ of
output tokens are a priori present as contiguous input spans, the act of copying them should not cost
the same as the act of generating new ones. Concretely:
Grammar over two primitives. We replace free-form output with a programmatic grammar
program := ’<program>’ (copy | gen)* ’</program>’
copy := ’<copy lines="i-j"/>’
gen := ’<gen>’ free_text ’</gen>’

enforced by a token-level finite-state machine that restricts the model’s logits to tokens whose
decoded prefix is consistent with the current grammar state. The decoder has three branches at each
op boundary (start a copy, start a gen, end the program); inside a copy op the model picks only the
numeric line indices; inside a gen op the model runs free until </gen>. The grammar guarantees
100% parse rate by construction.
Copy spans cost one parallel prefill. After the model commits to <copy lines="i-j"/>, the
tokens for lines i..j are already known—they are literal tokens from the input. We splice them into
the output sequence and update the KV cache with a single parallel-prefill forward, skipping N
autoregressive decode steps for a span of N tokens. This shares the parallel-forward acceleration
primitive of speculative decoding [1, 13, 25] but replaces probabilistic verification with grammar2

enforced acceptance: input tokens serve as the “draft” with acceptance probability 1 by construction.
The quality trade-off lives entirely in span selection.
Two quantitative bounds + one correctness property, without end-to-end training. The mechanism decomposes into three independently measurable properties. Two are quantitative bounds
on the payoff any copy-aware decoder can achieve (kernel speedup and copy ceiling); the third is a
correctness precondition, not an independent bound (pipeline losslessness—without it an EM failure
cannot be attributed to span selection). Composed, the first two yield the span-distribution-aware
exact bound bndexact (Table 2) that defines the payoff envelope any future trained system would have
to fit inside. None of the three requires training a span selector.
1. Kernel speedup (§4.1). For spans of length 8–512 and a 1024-token prefix on Qwen2.5-1.5B /
7B (single-sequence A100 80GB bf16), a parallel-prefill forward is 6.8×–303× faster than an
autoregressive loop over the same tokens. Speedup grows approximately linearly with span length
in the overhead-dominated regime and saturates at the compute-bound regime.
2. Copy ceiling (§4.2). For ProbeEdit (154 short-text edits) and HumanEvalPack-Fix (164 Python
+ 164 JS bug fixes), 74–98% of gold-output tokens are realizable as contiguous line-level copy
spans under oracle alignment—the ceiling for the mechanism as defined in §2. Composed with the
measured kernel s(N ) curve over each corpus’s actual span histogram, this yields the exact closedform wall-clock bound bndexact = 29.0× (ProbeEdit), 3.4× (HEvalFix-Py), 4.2× (HEvalFix-JS),
13.0× pooled. A token-level contiguous-span cover (an aspirational upper bound, not the current
primitive) reaches 91–99% with conservative floors at 4.5–6.5×, motivating the natural extension
to sub-line copy discussed in §7.
3. Pipeline losslessness (§4.3). With oracle programs induced from difflib.SequenceMatcher
alignment of gold to input, the deterministic resolver reproduces gold on all 482 cases across three
corpora under byte-equal comparison (up to a single trailing newline); whitespace-trimmed EM is
also 482/482. This is an identifiability precondition, not a payoff bound: any downstream exactmatch failure is therefore a model span-selection problem, not a mechanism bug. A perturbation
study (Table 8) shows the mechanism is unforgiving: pooled EM drops from 100% to 15.48%
under off-by-one noise on oracle line indices.
Kernel speedup and copy ceiling are systems and data properties that do not depend on model quality;
pipeline losslessness establishes that the resolver faithfully inverts an oracle program. Closing the
gap between the oracle ceiling and a realized deployed system is a model-training question—picking
the right spans—that we scope as follow-up work (§7). The perturbation study in §5 quantifies how
tight that selector has to be; it is a hardness diagnosis, not itself a feasibility result. A prompt-level
variant of the grammar (the only contribution of the paper superseded by this one, CRP) is retained as
an ablation for closed-model deployment without KV-cache access (Appendix Q).

sections.heading: Method: Copy-as-Decode
sections.text:
Copy-as-Decode sits at the intersection of structured constrained decoding and speculative decoding
(Figure 1). The mechanism has three components—a two-primitive grammar, a token-level finitestate machine that enforces it, and a parallel-prefill splice that realizes a copy span in one forward
pass—each introduced below.
2.1

Grammar and Problem Formulation

Given an input document D = l1 l2 · · · ln (indexed by lines) and an edit instruction I, the goal is to
produce the edited document D′ . Rather than autoregressively generating D′ token by token, we
have the model emit a program over a two-primitive grammar:
Program ::= <program> Op∗ </program>
Op ::= Copy | Gen
Copy ::= <copy lines="i-j"/>
Gen ::= <gen> F REE T EXT </gen>
A deterministic resolver R consumes a Program P and the immutable input D, and yields D′ =
R(P, D). Line indices reference the original D (no renumbering after edits).

2.2

Resolver Semantics

The resolver is deterministic and pure:
4

1. For each <copy lines="i-j"/> op, emit the verbatim text of li · · · lj from D, joined by newlines.
2. For each <gen>s</gen> op, emit s with at most one leading and one trailing newline stripped (a
readability allowance, preserving internal blank lines).
3. Concatenate ops with a single newline separator.
The resolver’s default behavior on out-of-range or malformed indices is to raise, but a single flag
toggles between strict (raise on any malformed op) and clipped (clip indices to [1, n], emit a warning)
semantics—we benchmark both modes explicitly in Table 4. It has no nondeterminism and no
dependence on the model. §4.3 measures pipeline losslessness: on all 482 (doc, gold) pairs across
three corpora, oracle programs induced from line-level alignment reconstruct gold exactly under strict
semantics—the strict-vs-clipped distinction matters only at deployment under a model that can emit
invalid indices, not for the oracle-derivation pipeline itself.
Reserved literals and principled escape. The grammar’s five structural substrings (<copy,
</copy>, <gen>, </gen>, </program>) must not appear verbatim inside a <gen>-body. We handle
this in two complementary places:
• Preprocessing escape. Each reserved substring in gold is replaced by a Unicode entity (e.g.
</gen>→〈/gen〉 via U+27E8/U+27E9/U+2024, unused by all tokenizers we checked); resolver
reverses before emit. For any gold g, decode(encode(g)) = g and encode is injective on inputs
free of the entities—holds on 482/482 cases and 10,000 adversarial fuzz strings (Appendix I).
• FSM end-of-gen detector. Exact token-id-sequence match against the 3-token Qwen BPE encoding
of </gen>, not a substring check on decoded text. Byte-level overlaps split across token boundaries
cannot mis-trigger the detector (Appendix I).
2.3

Token-Level Grammar-Constrained Decoder

A free-form decoder cannot be trusted to emit a valid Program: after a copy-span splice it has
just “seen itself output” a long run of document-like tokens and naturally continues regenerating
content. We enforce the grammar at the token level via a small FSM (5 states: AWAIT_OP, AFTER_LT,
COPY_LINES, GEN_BODY, CLOSE; see Appendix A) that intersects the model’s logits with the set of
tokens consistent with the current state. For Qwen2.5-family tokenizers (and any BPE tokenizer
encoding the structural literals as fixed token sequences), the relevant token ids are fixed constants.
The FSM alternates three step types:
• Masked model steps at decision points: argmax restricted to {<, </} at op boundaries; {copy, gen}
for op type; digits plus -/" inside a copy’s line range.
• Forced-template prefills for fixed literal sequences (_lines=", "/>, </gen>, </program>), each
spliced via a single parallel-prefill forward.
• Free generation inside <gen> bodies until the 3-token Qwen encoding of </gen> is produced
(Appendix I).
The structural portion is therefore never subject to model error; the model chooses only op types, line
indices, and <gen>-body content. Parse rate is 100% by construction.
2.4

Copy-Span Splicing via Parallel Prefill

When the FSM exits the copy-line-index state with a chosen range [i, j], we tokenize li · · · lj directly
from D and append those tokens to the KV cache in a single forward pass:
model(input_ids = [[li · · · lj ]], past_key_values = KV)
This is an ordinary transformer prefill forward over N = |[[li · · · lj ]]| tokens, not N decode forwards.
The forward still computes all self-attention and feed-forward activations over the N tokens, but
it does so in parallel within one launch, amortizing the per-step kernel overhead and, on modern
hardware, running in the GEMM-bound regime rather than the memory-bandwidth-bound regime
typical of single-token decode.

an identifiability precondition rather than a payoff bound. Table 1 consolidates the measurement

sections.heading: Results
sections.text:
We present three measurable properties: (i) kernel speedup (what a single copy splice buys in wallclock, §4.1), (ii) copy ceiling (how often copy-heavy structure is actually present in editing data, §4.2),
and (iii) pipeline losslessness (the resolver reproduces gold from oracle programs, §4.3). The first two
are quantitative bounds; composing them yields the exact, span-distribution-aware wall-clock upper
bound bndexact on any copy-aware decoder for these corpora (Table 2). The third is a correctness
property, not an independent payoff bound—without it a downstream EM failure cannot be attributed
to span selection. All three are data-level / systems-level properties of the mechanism; none requires
an end-to-end trained model.
4.1

Kernel Speedup

Figure 3 reports per-span speedup across span lengths 1–512 tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B. At
N = 8 the speedup is already 6.8× (7B) / 7.0× (1.5B), and it grows monotonically with N up to
90.5× (7B, N = 512) and 303× (1.5B, N = 512).
Two regimes. Below N ≈ 64, per-step decode is dominated by kernel-launch and memory-transfer
overhead, and parallel prefill is N -times-plus-a-small-constant faster. Above N ≈ 128, the 7B
curve saturates as parallel-prefill enters the compute-bound regime, while the 1.5B curve remains
overhead-dominated because its per-layer GEMM is small relative to memory-movement fixed cost.
This matches the crossover documented for speculative-decoding verification forwards [1, 13]. At
N ∈ {1, 2} parallel prefill and autoregressive are within ≈ 1.1–1.3×; the splice is only worth
invoking above m = 8. Measurements are single-sequence (batch 1) on eager HuggingFace attention;
integration with vLLM paged attention is future work (§7).

4.3

Pipeline Losslessness

Oracle programs are derived by deterministic difflib.SequenceMatcher line-level alignment (no
model) and resolved through the same code path invoked at deployment. Reconstruction is byte-exact
on all 482/482 cases across ProbeEdit (154), HEvalFix-Py (164), and HEvalFix-JS (164), under both
byte-exact (tolerant of a single trailing newline) and trimmed (.strip()) equality. A grammar-literal
audit finds 0/482 gold outputs containing the reserved substrings </gen> or <copy. This establishes:
(i) the resolver is lossless on all cases up to at most a single trailing newline; (ii) any downstream
exact-match failure decomposes as span-selection error, not resolver error; (iii) the naive grammar
suffices on these corpora, though general-purpose deployment requires the principled escape of §2.2.

Span-selection brittleness. Perfect line-level span selection round-trips to gold on all 482 oracle
cases (§4.3); how tight must a realized selector be? We perturb each oracle CopyLines endpoint by
integer noise ∼ Uniform[−ϵ, +ϵ], clamp to the valid document range, and re-run the resolver.
Figure 6 shows the collapse is sharp: at ϵ=1 (each line index off by at most one line) trimmed EM
drops from 100% to 9–25% across corpora. Line-level addressing is an unforgiving representation—
small index errors do not produce small output errors—unlike token-matching apply tools where
a near-match on the anchor still localizes the edit. A deployed selector must achieve near-perfect
per-copy endpoint accuracy to realize the oracle ceiling; the 100% → 9–25% gap at ϵ=1 is the
operational target any subsequent span-selection training must hit.
Selector learnability pilot. The perturbation study is a hardness diagnosis, not a deployability
result. To locate where a small-scale trained selector sits relative to that hardness, we fine-tune
Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct (full-parameter, bf16; AdamW, lr 2×10−5 ; cosine schedule) to emit
oracle programs. Two training sets are used: Py-only (131 HEvalFix-Py examples, 8 epochs) and
Combined (385 examples pooling Py + JS + ProbeEdit, 6 epochs). Each is repeated across seeds
{0, 1, 2}. Evaluation is on 33 HEvalFix-Py held-out cases with FSM-constrained greedy decoding;
mean EM is reported as fractions (successes/attempts) with Wilson 95% CI.
Table 6 reports three findings. (1) The selector is learnable at small scale: 131 oracle programs
lift held-out EM from 0/33 (every untrained strategy, including prompt-level and FSM-constrained
baselines) to 12/99 = 12.1% (Wilson 95% CI [7.0, 20.1]); span-endpoint accuracy crosses out of the
ϵ=5 regime of Figure 6. (2) Data scale helps weakly: pooling Py + JS + ProbeEdit (385 cases, 6
epochs) lifts EM to 17/99 = 17.2% (Wilson 95% CI [11.0, 26.0]), a +5.1-pp point estimate with
overlapping intervals (not a significant effect at n=99; p=0.32, χ2 ). (3) Endpoint error is the
dominant failure mode: 64–75% of held-out attempts have at least one endpoint off by ≥ 1 line
(Table 7), and op-level span-start accuracy (0.64–0.66) exceeds span-end (0.45–0.51) by ≈ 15 pp
across configurations, mirroring the same ordering in untrained baselines. End-of-copy boundary is
harder than start-of-copy because it localizes where a preserved run terminates under an edit—a less
locally-cued decision. This identifies the highest-leverage sub-task for follow-up training.
What 12–17% EM means for deployment. The headline number is a learnability signal at the
smallest viable training scale, not an accuracy claim. Three operational caveats:
• Statistical: Wilson 95% CI upper bound is 26.0%; at n=99 we cannot distinguish the selector
from a ≤ 26% system. A deployment decision needs either larger n or a downstream task where
15–25% correct-edit rate is already useful (e.g. multi-attempt refactoring with rejection sampling).
• Expected-speedup gap: the gap to bndexact =3.45× on HEvalFix-Py is not the 82.8-pp absolute
EM gap but the realized-copy-fraction gap. A partial selector that gets nEM cases right contributes
the full bndexact on those and falls back to full regeneration on the rest, yielding ≈ 1 + (nEM /n) ·

Pointer-decoder baseline. A natural architectural alternative is a span-level pointer decoder [26]:
attach three classification heads to a base LM (op-type, span-start, span-end), training end-to-end to
emit the same {COPY, GEN} op sequence without serializing through XML text. The information
content per COPY op is identical—two small integers—so selector-EM should match C OPY- AS D ECODE. Where they differ is fixed cost per op: a span-level pointer pays 3 autoregressive forward
passes (op-type+start+end), while C OPY- AS -D ECODE pays 2 (FSM open/close) + 1 (forced template
prefill) + N/s(N ) (parallel-prefill splice) = 3 + N/s(N ). The pointer is therefore strictly cheaper
in fixed overhead (by ≈ 0.15 forward-pass-equivalents per copy op on our corpora; see Appendix L),
but requires dedicated training and dedicated heads, while C OPY- AS -D ECODE is a format layered
on any instruction-tuned LM. A token-level pointer (predict input-position at every copied token) is
strictly dominated: N forward passes vs N/s(N ). The mechanism claim is thus not “copy is free”—a
span-level pointer achieves that with architectural surgery—but “copy can be made format-level and
still get most of the way there,” which is the deployable property.
Composition with speculative decoding. The splice accelerates copy regions; speculative decoding [13, 14] accelerates generation regions. The two are orthogonal and compose multiplicatively.
Under the extended cost model (Appendix H), a gen region of n tokens costs 2 + n AR steps without
speculation and 2 + n/sspec with; copy regions are unaffected. Using the measured Qwen2.5-7B
splice curve (Table 11) and a conservative sspec =2.5× (middle of the 2–3× range typically reported
on code [14]), the combined predicted speedup over full regeneration rises from 22.4× to 27.1× on

Token-level extension. The line-level primitive caps the oracle copy fraction at 74–91% (Table 2);
a token-level primitive <copy tokens="a-b"/>, referencing token indices directly, is a straightforward generalization (Appendix N). Running the same oracle-derivation pipeline on token granularity
under the Qwen2.5-Coder-7B BPE raises the achievable copy fraction to 98.6% (ProbeEdit), 92.7%
(HEvalFix-Py), and 94.5% (HEvalFix-JS), round-tripping byte-exact on ≥ 95% of cases where the
tokenizer is itself lossless over the text pair. The trade-off: the model must select token boundaries
rather than line boundaries (smaller unit, tighter precision), which raises the empirical selectionaccuracy bar sharply (Figure 6 extrapolates). We leave realized token-level selector training to future
work and report the ceiling here as the ceiling C OPY- AS -D ECODE’s mechanism admits.
What this does not establish. At 14–17% EM the pilot is below any production threshold. It
demonstrates learnability of the line-level representation at commodity scale and portability of the
gain across two languages and one text corpus (within ±3 pp; Appendix O), not a deployable system.
The closed-model prompt-level variant (§Q) reaches 80% EM on GPT-5-mini, upper-bounding what a
constrained-decoding variant on a comparable-capability base can achieve when the FSM additionally
guarantees parse rate. Scaling the SFT pilot to 7B (multi-seed, full-parameter) and larger corpora is
the first item in §7.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.text:
Speculative decoding and draft-based acceleration. Blockwise parallel decoding [25] first observed that a single parallel forward can verify multiple draft tokens at once; speculative decoding [3, 13, 28] generalized this with a draft-model/target-model distinction and a probabilistic
acceptance rule that preserves the target distribution. Medusa [1] replaces the separate draft model
with extra prediction heads on the target; EAGLE [14, 15] drafts in feature space rather than token
space; SpecInfer [19] extends to tree-based draft expansion; Yang et al. [29], Zhang et al. [30] explore
multi-candidate and self-drafting variants; REST [10] retrieves drafts from a corpus. Across this
family, drafts are produced by some learned predictor and accepted probabilistically to preserve the
target distribution.
Copy-as-Decode shares the parallel-forward primitive but differs in two architectural respects: the
“draft” is the input document (not a smaller-model prediction) selected by grammar commitment, and
acceptance is unconditional (not probabilistic)—so Copy-as-Decode does not preserve speculative
decoding’s free-form target distribution, redefining the decoded task as an edit program. In exchange
it avoids draft-model training and obtains a trivial parallel-forward ratio equal to the AR-vs-PP kernel
ratio. The two methods compose: within a <gen> body, any speculative-decoding scheme can further
accelerate free-text generation.
Prompt-lookup decoding and input-aware drafting. The closest prior mechanism is promptlookup decoding [22]: draft candidate continuations by suffix-matching against the prompt and
15

accept them via the ordinary speculative-decoding verification rule. Input-conditioned retrievaldrafting [10, 22] is in the same family—drafts sourced from input or corpus, acceptance probabilistic.

Edit-as-program paradigms. Casting editing as emitting a program over the input has precedent
outside decoder-accelerated serving; they differ in granularity and in whether the program is applied
at decode-time or post-decode:
• String-level: search/replace (Aider [6]) and unified-diff apply.
• Per-token tag: LaserTagger [18], FELIX [17], GECToR [21].
• Prompt-level line-reference: CRP [16].
• Decode-time line-reference, KV-splicing (ours): Copy-as-Decode.
What distinguishes this work is the coupling between program form and serving primitive: the
line-reference program is chosen so the deterministic resolver realizes as a parallel-prefill KV-cache
splice over the model’s own KV, not a post-decode string application. The format-cost head-to-head
of Table 3 and the kernel measurement of Figure 3 are the two halves of this coupling; no prior
edit-as-program paradigm offers the second half.

Constrained decoding. Structured constrained decoding enforces an output grammar at the token
level: PICARD [23] monitors partial SQL for well-formedness; Outlines [27] formulates decoding
as finite-state intersection by compiling regular expressions and context-free grammars into tokenlevel FSMs with a vocabulary index; XGrammar [5] and SGLang [31] provide efficient parallel-safe
grammar compilation; Geng et al. [7] extends this to unconstrained LMs by masking with EBNF/CFG
grammars without fine-tuning. Our FSM (§2.3) is a small instance of this family: an FSM over the
16

<copy>/<gen> grammar, made efficient by exploiting that Qwen-family BPE tokenizers encode each
structural literal as a fixed multi-token sequence. What is distinctive is not the FSM itself but that the
FSM serves a dual role—guaranteeing parse rate and marking the points at which the parallel-prefill
splice can be invoked.
Grammar-engine masking overhead. A parallel line of systems work focuses on driving per-step
mask construction near zero: XGrammar [5] compiles a context-free grammar into an adaptive
token-mask cache; SGLang [31] amortizes mask computation across requests via runtime sharing.
Our FSM sits at the lower bound of this cost spectrum: 5 states, at most 12 allowed token-ids
at any masked step (Figure 7 and Appendix A), measured at cmask = 0.02 ms per masked step
on Qwen2.5-1.5B (Appendix H)—two orders of magnitude below a single decode step. Copy-asDecode’s grammar-constrained path is therefore compatible with any of the above engines and adds
no measurable masking overhead; the substantive cost is the parallel-prefill splice, which none of
these engines provide.
Edit formats and apply models. Production tools use a variety of output formats for code and
document edits. Aider [6] uses search/replace blocks, where the model emits both the verbatim text
to find and the verbatim text to replace; unified-diff emits the standard @@ hunk format used by git.
Cursor’s instant-apply [4] and Anthropic’s text-editor tool are closed-model apply pipelines whose
training recipes are not public. Related work on editing as a task—SWE-bench [11], CanItEdit [2],
HumanEvalPack [20]—evaluates end-to-end correctness rather than the decoding mechanism itself.
All of these require the model to re-emit structural context (search anchors, hunk headers, or the entire
edited span) through ordinary autoregressive decoding. Copy-as-Decode differs in replacing the
model-produced reference with a grammar-enforced one, and in splicing the referenced tokens into
the KV cache rather than paying decode cost for them. §4.4 benchmarks these formats head-to-head
on a unified parse+apply harness: search/replace matches our format-theoretic token budget but loses
6–19% of cases to anchor ambiguity, while unified diff matches our round-trip fidelity but costs
17–64% more tokens per edit.
Copy mechanisms at the architectural level. Pointer networks [26] and copy mechanisms [8, 24]
augment encoder-decoder generation with a learned pointer distribution over input positions. Edit-astagging architectures—LaserTagger [18], FELIX [17], GECToR [21]—cast editing as classifying
each input token with an operation. The Levenshtein Transformer [9] learns non-autoregressive
insertion/deletion operations. These approaches modify the model itself. Copy-as-Decode instead
operates at the decoding and serving layer: any pretrained autoregressive LM that can be coaxed to
emit the <copy>/<gen> grammar under the FSM can be served with it.
Prompt-level structured output for edits. Closed-model structured-output prompting [16] has
been studied as an edit format—the model emits a line-referencing program that a deterministic
resolver expands. Our earlier work on CRP falls in this category; we treat it here as the prompt-level
variant of Copy-as-Decode (Appendix Q) that retains the output-token compression benefit but not
the wall-clock kernel speedup. The mechanism-level contribution of this paper is the combination of
grammar-constrained decoding, parallel-prefill splicing, and a lossless resolver.

sections.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text:
We recast edit generation as structured decoding over a two-primitive grammar, enforced by a tokenlevel FSM and accelerated by a parallel-prefill splice that replaces N autoregressive decode steps
with one forward. The contribution is the mechanism together with three measurable properties—two
quantitative bounds and one correctness property—independent of model quality: (i) one parallelprefill forward is 6.8×–303× faster than N autoregressive decodes for N ∈ [8, 512] on Qwen2.5{1.5B, 7B}; (ii) 74–98% of gold tokens are realizable under the line-level primitive on ProbeEdit
and HumanEvalPack-Fix, which composed with the kernel curve over each corpus’s exact span
histogram yields the closed-form wall-clock bound bndexact = 29.0 × /3.4 × /4.2× (ProbeEdit / Py
/ JS, 13.0× pooled); (iii) oracle programs round-trip byte-exactly on all 482 cases—an identifiability
precondition that localizes any downstream EM failure to span selection. A perturbation study
(pooled EM 100% → 15.48% under off-by-one noise) gives an operational target for any trained
selector.
17

Scope. In scope: contiguous line-range copy (and, in the token-level extension of §5, contiguous
token-range copy) from a single input document to a single output document, with K ≤ 20 ops per edit
on the evaluated corpora. Out of scope for the present paper: multi-file and agentic workloads (SWEbench-style); AST-granular edits whose operands are subtrees rather than spans; splice integration
into the vLLM/SGLang scheduler (format-only latency gains on vLLM 0.19 continuous batching are
measured in §4.5; paged-attention splice integration is scaffolded in Appendix K and deferred).
Limitations and future work. The FSM’s fixed-id table is tokenizer-conditional and resolved
once at load (Appendix K: ≥ 7/14 of our structural literals are single-token across Qwen2.5,
DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama-family tokenizers; fragmented tokenizers add ≈ 0.02 ms per
literal). Reserved-literal substrings in gold are handled by a principled Unicode-entity escape (§2.2,
I), so “the gold-audit holds on our corpora” is no longer the load-bearing claim. Line granularity
loses coverage to sub-expression rewrites; the 74–98% vs. 93–99% line-vs-token gap (Table 2,
Appendix N) is closed by the token-indexed <copy tokens> primitive, which we formalize and
measure as an oracle-ceiling in this draft but whose realized selector training we defer. The pilot
selector at 14–18% EM is a learnability signal, not a deployment result. Four concrete follow-ups:
(i) scale the selector to 7B QLoRA with larger corpora and span-end-targeted supervision (span-end
accuracy is the dominant error, §5); (ii) productize the token-level <copy tokens> primitive under
a trained selector; (iii) integrate the splice into vLLM/SGLang continuous batching with paged
attention and report E2E latency/throughput at realistic QPS, above the format-only 2.1–3.3× floor
we measure in §4.5; (iv) apply in code-editing agent loops and on SWE-bench-style benchmarks.
